title: A youth-heavy demographic wave turns jobs into an infrastructure, sector, and social-stability challenge
source_unit: World Bank, The Global Jobs Challenge
geography: Emerging market and developing economies, with global demographic, labor-market, infrastructure, and sector implications

denominator.unit: young people in emerging market and developing economies expected to reach working age

development_stakes.value: sufficient job creation could support poverty reduction, shared prosperity, self-sufficient economies, and social stability

challenge_condition.value: many affected economies enter the demographic wave with low per-capita incomes, high debt, and limited policy room

observations.method: World Bank synthesis of demographic projections, labor-market conditions, macroeconomic constraints, infrastructure, and job-creation policy pathways.
observations.uncertainty: The projection describes a demographic opportunity and pressure, not a forecast of actual employment, earnings, migration, or political behavior in every country.
observations.subgroup: Young people entering working age, households, employers, governments, migrants, and communities in emerging market and developing economies.
observations.counterinterpretation: A large working-age cohort can raise growth and innovation when education, health, institutions, finance, and job demand align; demographic size alone does not determine outcomes.

denominator.unit: World Bank global jobs policy framework

policy_pillars.value: foundational physical, human, and digital capital; a business-friendly environment; and mobilization of private capital

structural_pressure.value: slower global growth, harder export-led strategies, AI, and the energy transition complicate job creation

coordination_need.value: national strategies need to be adapted to country circumstances while international support remains relevant

observations.method: World Bank policy synthesis connecting labor demand to physical infrastructure, human capital, digital access, firms, finance, and national strategy.
observations.uncertainty: The framework identifies enabling conditions but does not estimate the cost, sequencing, or country-specific employment effect of each pillar.
observations.subgroup: Workers, job seekers, firms, investors, training systems, infrastructure users, governments, and development-finance institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Private capital and business reform can expand opportunity but may not reach lagging regions or vulnerable workers without public investment, labor protections, and inclusive access.

denominator.unit: sectors identified by the World Bank as having potential for resilient, large-scale job creation

sector_set.value: infrastructure including energy, agribusiness and farming, health, tourism, and value-added manufacturing

cross_domain_link.value: job creation depends on connections among physical systems, food production, care, mobility, services, and industrial upgrading

resilience_frame.value: sector strategies are presented as part of resilient, large-scale job creation rather than a single-industry solution

observations.method: World Bank comparison of sector opportunities within a global jobs and development framework.
observations.uncertainty: Sector potential varies with local demand, productivity, skills, energy and transport access, environmental constraints, trade conditions, and institutional quality.
observations.subgroup: Workers, farmers, caregivers, health workers, tourism workers, manufacturers, entrepreneurs, consumers, and communities near infrastructure or industrial investment.
observations.counterinterpretation: Sector expansion can create low-quality or insecure work and environmental pressure unless productivity gains are paired with rights, skills, public services, and distributional safeguards.

observations.period: 2026 onward; jobs, poverty, and social stability

welfare_route.value: jobs are presented as central to reducing poverty and promoting shared prosperity

stability_route.value: employment opportunity is linked to self-sufficient economies and social stability

technology_transition.value: AI and the energy transition create uncertainty alongside potential productivity and investment opportunities

observations.method: World Bank synthesis linking demographic change, employment, poverty, macroeconomic conditions, technology, energy, and social stability.
observations.uncertainty: The publication does not establish that job growth alone causes social stability or that technology transitions will produce net gains for every worker or place.
observations.subgroup: Young workers, informal workers, households, firms, governments, communities facing economic frustration, and people affected by AI or energy-transition restructuring.
observations.counterinterpretation: Social stability also depends on rights, representation, prices, public services, identity, conflict, and political legitimacy; employment indicators should not substitute for those dimensions.

related_sources.claim: World Bank climate-and-jobs analysis provides complementary evidence on adaptation, employment shifts, and resilience investment.
World Bank demographic-trends analysis provides complementary evidence on age structure, labor, migration, and development policy.

boundary: This record adds a global jobs route linking youth demography, infrastructure, human and digital capital, private finance, priority sectors, technology transitions, poverty, and social stability. It is a publication-level synthesis, not individual employment histories, respondent-level labor data, a country job forecast, or proof that any single policy creates stability.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official World Bank Global Jobs Challenge page was reviewed for the 2025-2035 youth cohort, policy pillars, structural constraints, priority sectors, and jobs-to-stability pathways.
